ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: Sudden, severe left-sided headache that began ~4 hours ago.
• Symptom details:
  – Onset: Abrupt this morning, first episode of this kind.
  – Location: Left side of head, sometimes described ‘behind the eye.’
  – Severity: 6/10 (kidney-stone pain =10/10 reference).
  – Associated features: Blurred vision with zig-zag lines (visual aura), dizziness, photophobia (can’t look at screens), nausea and 2 episodes of vomiting, feels worse when moving the head, prefers lying still.
  – Aggravating/alleviating: Movement worsens; paracetamol taken 3 h ago gave no relief.
• Past medical history: Kidney stones; no prior migraines.
• Medications: None.  Paracetamol tried today.
• Allergies: Denies known drug allergies.
• Family history: Mother – migraines and hypothyroidism.
• Social / obstetric: Pregnancy unlikely (patient statement). No other social history given.
• Vital signs / physical exam: Tele-visit; no vitals supplied. Patient reports no focal weakness, normal gait.
• Labs / imaging: None performed or mentioned.

V: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH): Sudden onset, worst ‘first’ headache + nausea/vomiting could represent thunderclap bleed.
Carotid/vertebral artery dissection: Unilateral headache, visual symptoms, dizziness.
I: Acute viral/bacterial meningitis: Headache, nausea/vomiting, photophobia; could begin suddenly.
Encephalitis: Similar symptom cluster with altered vision/dizziness.
N: Intracranial mass (e.g., brain tumour): New headache with visual changes raises concern in patient; less likely with abrupt onset.
D: Cervical spondylosis tension-type headache: Possible but onset usually gradual, lacks aura.
I2: Medication/withdrawal headache (e.g., caffeine withdrawal): Headache ± nausea, but visual aura less typical.
C: Arteriovenous malformation: Could present with sudden headache if bleeding or steal phenomenon.
A: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri): Headache, visual disturbance, nausea/vomiting, common in young females.
T: Post-traumatic intracranial bleed: Not supported by history of trauma.
E: Migraine with aura: Unilateral throbbing headache, visual zig-zag lines, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, family history.
Cluster headache: Unilateral severe pain behind eye, but usually male, shorter attacks, autonomic features.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Fits classic description: unilateral headache, visual zig-zag aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, moderate pain, positive family history.
supporting_evidence: Visual symptoms – blurred vision with zig-zag lines (typical aura)
Nausea and two episodes of vomiting
opposing_evidence: First lifetime episode at age 33 (later than usual though still possible)
Abrupt onset might suggest vascular cause

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Any sudden severe ‘first’ headache demands exclusion of SAH; associated nausea/vomiting and dizziness overlap.
supporting_evidence: Abrupt onset this morning (‘came on suddenly’)
Patient perceives pain as unusually intense/new
opposing_evidence: Pain rated 6/10, not the ‘worst ever’ thunderclap description
No neck stiffness, photophobia mild, no altered consciousness
Normal speech, gait, no neuro deficit reported

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young adults with unilateral headache and visual disturbance can present this way; dizziness also noted.
opposing_evidence: No neck pain or trauma history
No focal neurological deficits (e.g., Horner’s, limb weakness)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Headache, nausea/vomiting and photophobia could represent meningitis.
opposing_evidence: No fever or neck stiffness reported
Able to converse normally, no confusion

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient worry; tumours usually produce progressive, not sudden, headaches; still on differential for new headache with visual issues.
supporting_evidence: New onset headache with visual change
opposing_evidence: Acute onset over hours not typical for tumour
No chronic morning headaches, seizures, neuro deficits
